cards.front: Before using SOHCAHTOA, what type of triangle must the diagram contain?

options.explanation: SOHCAHTOA defines trigonometric ratios using the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse sides of a right-angled triangle, which must contain a $90^\circ$ angle.
An acute-angled triangle has no $90^\circ$ angle, so the standard SOHCAHTOA side relationships do not apply directly. The diagram must contain a right-angled triangle.
An obtuse-angled triangle contains an angle greater than $90^\circ$, rather than a right angle. Basic SOHCAHTOA requires a right-angled triangle.
An equilateral triangle has three $60^\circ$ angles and therefore no hypotenuse. Basic SOHCAHTOA requires a right-angled triangle.

cards.front: If a side is opposite the $90^\circ$ angle, what is its label?

options.explanation: The side directly opposite the $90^\circ$ angle is always the hypotenuse. It is also the longest side of a right-angled triangle.
The opposite side is identified relative to the chosen acute angle, not the $90^\circ$ angle. The side opposite $90^\circ$ is the hypotenuse.
The adjacent side lies beside the chosen acute angle and is not the hypotenuse. The side opposite the $90^\circ$ angle is the hypotenuse.
“Base” may describe a side’s position in a drawing, but it is not the required trigonometric label. The side opposite $90^\circ$ is the hypotenuse.

cards.front: From the chosen angle, a side directly across has what label?

options.explanation: The side directly across from the chosen acute angle is labelled the opposite side because it does not touch that angle.
The adjacent side touches the chosen angle, whereas the side directly across from that angle is labelled the opposite side.
The hypotenuse is specifically the side opposite the $90^\circ$ angle, not necessarily the side across from the chosen acute angle. That side is opposite.
“Base” describes how a diagram may be drawn rather than the side’s relationship to the chosen angle. The side directly across is the opposite side.

cards.front: From the chosen angle, what is the non-hypotenuse side next to it called?

options.explanation: The adjacent side touches the chosen acute angle and is not the hypotenuse. Its label can change when a different focus angle is selected.
The opposite side lies directly across from the chosen angle rather than next to it. The non-hypotenuse side touching the angle is adjacent.
The hypotenuse touches each acute angle, but it is excluded by the question and is always opposite $90^\circ$. The other neighbouring side is adjacent.
“Base” depends on the triangle’s orientation and is not a SOHCAHTOA side label. The non-hypotenuse side next to the chosen angle is adjacent.

cards.front: Changing the focus angle can swap [ ___ ], but the [ ___ ] stays the same.
cards.back: Changing the focus angle can swap opposite and adjacent, but the hypotenuse stays the same.

options.text: Changing the focus angle can swap opposite and adjacent, but the hypotenuse stays the same.
options.explanation: Opposite and adjacent are defined relative to the selected acute angle, so they can exchange labels. The hypotenuse remains opposite the fixed $90^\circ$ angle.

options.text: Changing the focus angle can swap hypotenuse and adjacent, but the hypotenuse stays the same.
options.explanation: The hypotenuse is fixed as the side opposite $90^\circ$, so it cannot swap with the adjacent side. Only opposite and adjacent depend on the focus angle.

options.text: Changing the focus angle can swap opposite and adjacent, but the opposite stays the same.
options.explanation: Although opposite and adjacent can swap when the focus angle changes, the opposite side does not remain fixed. The hypotenuse always stays the same.

options.text: Changing the focus angle can swap opposite and hypotenuse, but the adjacent stays the same.
options.explanation: The hypotenuse cannot become an angle-dependent side, and the adjacent side does not remain fixed. Opposite and adjacent swap, while the hypotenuse stays unchanged.

cards.front: $$\sin\theta$ uses [ ___ ] over [ ___ ].

options.explanation: The mnemonic SOH means sine equals opposite divided by hypotenuse, so $\sin\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$.
Adjacent over hypotenuse is the cosine ratio, represented by CAH. Sine follows SOH, so it uses opposite over hypotenuse.
Opposite over adjacent is the tangent ratio, represented by TOA. Sine follows SOH, so its denominator is the hypotenuse.
This reverses the sine ratio, producing the reciprocal of sine rather than sine itself. SOH gives opposite over hypotenuse.

cards.front: $$\cos\theta$ uses [ ___ ] over [ ___ ].

options.explanation: The mnemonic CAH means cosine equals adjacent divided by hypotenuse, so $\cos\theta=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$.
Opposite over hypotenuse is the sine ratio, represented by SOH. Cosine follows CAH, so it uses adjacent over hypotenuse.
Adjacent over opposite is the reciprocal of tangent, not cosine. CAH states that cosine uses adjacent over hypotenuse.
This reverses the cosine ratio, giving the reciprocal of cosine rather than cosine itself. CAH gives adjacent over hypotenuse.

cards.front: $$\tan\theta$ uses [ ___ ] over [ ___ ].

options.explanation: The mnemonic TOA means tangent equals opposite divided by adjacent, so $\tan\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$.
Opposite over hypotenuse is the sine ratio, not tangent. TOA shows that tangent uses opposite over adjacent.
Adjacent over hypotenuse is the cosine ratio, represented by CAH. Tangent follows TOA, so it uses opposite over adjacent.
This reverses the tangent ratio and gives the reciprocal of tangent. TOA places opposite above adjacent, not adjacent above opposite.

cards.front: What does $\theta$ usually mean in SOHCAHTOA?

options.explanation: The symbol $\theta$ conventionally represents the angle being considered. Identifying this angle allows the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse sides to be labelled correctly.
The hypotenuse is a side of the right-angled triangle, not the quantity represented by $\theta$. In SOHCAHTOA, $\theta$ normally denotes the angle being used.
The opposite side is identified relative to $\theta$, but it is not represented by that symbol. The symbol $\theta$ normally means the angle.
The right angle is fixed at $90^\circ$ and is usually marked with a square. The symbol $\theta$ normally denotes the other angle being considered.

cards.front: Angle $35^\circ$, opposite $20\text{ cm}$, hypotenuse $x$: what expression gives $x$?

options.explanation: Using $\sin\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ gives $\sin35^\circ=\frac{20}{x}$. Rearranging by multiplying by $x$ and dividing by $\sin35^\circ$ gives this expression.
This multiplies by the sine value instead of dividing by it. From $\sin35^\circ=\frac{20}{x}$, rearrangement gives $x=\frac{20}{\sin35^\circ}$.
Cosine relates the adjacent side to the hypotenuse, but the given side is opposite the angle. Sine is required, giving $x=\frac{20}{\sin35^\circ}$.
This reverses the quantities when rearranging and would not produce a length of the correct size. The hypotenuse is $x=\frac{20}{\sin35^\circ}$.

cards.front: Angle $42^\circ$, opposite $11\text{ cm}$, adjacent $x$: what expression gives $x$?

options.explanation: Using $\tan\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$ gives $\tan42^\circ=\frac{11}{x}$. Rearranging by multiplying by $x$ and dividing by $\tan42^\circ$ produces this expression.
This multiplies by the tangent value rather than dividing by it. Rearranging $\tan42^\circ=\frac{11}{x}$ gives $x=\frac{11}{\tan42^\circ}$.
Sine requires the opposite side and hypotenuse, but the known sides here are opposite and adjacent. Tangent must be used, giving $x=\frac{11}{\tan42^\circ}$.
This incorrectly reverses the numerator and denominator during rearrangement. Starting from $\tan42^\circ=\frac{11}{x}$ leads to $x=\frac{11}{\tan42^\circ}$.

cards.front: For IGCSE trigonometry, the calculator should normally be in [ ___ ] mode, not [ ___ ].
cards.back: For IGCSE trigonometry, the calculator should normally be in degrees mode, not radians.

options.text: For IGCSE trigonometry, the calculator should normally be in degrees mode, not radians.
options.explanation: IGCSE triangle angles are normally stated in degrees, as shown by the $^\circ$ symbol. Radian mode would therefore produce incorrect trigonometric values.

options.text: For IGCSE trigonometry, the calculator should normally be in radians mode, not degrees.
options.explanation: This reverses the required calculator settings. IGCSE triangle questions normally measure angles in degrees, so the calculator should use degrees rather than radians.

options.text: For IGCSE trigonometry, the calculator should normally be in gradians mode, not radians.
options.explanation: Gradians divide a full turn into 400 units and are not normally used in IGCSE triangle questions. The appropriate setting is degrees, not radians.

options.text: For IGCSE trigonometry, the calculator should normally be in radians mode, not gradians.
options.explanation: Radian mode is common in advanced mathematics but not for ordinary IGCSE triangle angles marked with $^\circ$. The calculator should normally use degrees, not gradians.

cards.front: If the angle is unknown, what type of trig button is usually needed?

options.explanation: When a side ratio is known and the angle is required, an inverse sine, cosine or tangent function reverses the relevant trigonometric relationship.
An ordinary trig button converts a known angle into a side ratio rather than recovering an angle. An inverse trig button is needed when the angle is unknown.
A logarithm button reverses exponentiation, not a trigonometric ratio. To recover an angle from a side ratio, the corresponding inverse trig button is required.
A square root button reverses squaring and cannot recover an angle from a trigonometric ratio. The required operation is an inverse trig function.

cards.front: Adjacent $16\text{ cm}$, hypotenuse $24\text{ cm}$, angle $x$: what inverse expression finds $x$?

options.explanation: Cosine uses adjacent over hypotenuse, so $\cos x=\frac{16}{24}$. Applying inverse cosine to both sides gives the required expression for $x$.
Sine uses opposite over hypotenuse, but $16$ is the adjacent side. Cosine is therefore required: $x=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{16}{24}\right)$.
This reverses adjacent over hypotenuse, producing a ratio greater than $1$, for which inverse cosine has no real angle. The ratio must be $\frac{16}{24}$.
Ordinary cosine converts an angle into a ratio; it does not convert a ratio back into an angle. The inverse expression is $x=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{16}{24}\right)$.

cards.front: Opposite $11\text{ cm}$, adjacent $15\text{ cm}$, angle $x$: what inverse expression finds $x$?

options.explanation: Tangent uses opposite over adjacent, so $\tan x=\frac{11}{15}$. Applying inverse tangent gives the angle expression shown.
This reverses the tangent ratio by placing adjacent over opposite. Tangent requires opposite over adjacent, so the correct expression uses $\frac{11}{15}$.
Inverse sine requires an opposite-to-hypotenuse ratio, but $15$ is the adjacent side. With opposite and adjacent known, use $x=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{11}{15}\right)$.
Inverse cosine requires an adjacent-to-hypotenuse ratio, but $11$ and $15$ are opposite and adjacent. Their correct relationship is tangent, using opposite over adjacent.

cards.front: Inverse trig works backwards from a side ratio to find an [ ___ ]; $\tan^{-1}$ does not mean [ ___ ].
cards.back: Inverse trig works backwards from a side ratio to find an angle; $\tan^{-1}$ does not mean one divided by tangent.

options.text: Inverse trig works backwards from a side ratio to find an angle; $\tan^{-1}$ does not mean one divided by tangent.
options.explanation: An inverse trigonometric function converts a known side ratio back into its corresponding angle. The superscript $-1$ denotes an inverse function, not a reciprocal.

options.text: Inverse trig works backwards from a side ratio to find a side length; $\tan^{-1}$ does not mean one divided by tangent.
options.explanation: A side ratio and inverse trig function determine an angle, not a side length. The notation $\tan^{-1}$ means inverse tangent rather than one divided by tangent.

options.text: Inverse trig works backwards from a side ratio to find an angle; $\tan^{-1}$ does not mean inverse tangent.
options.explanation: Inverse trig does recover an angle, but the second statement wrongly denies the meaning of the notation. Here, $\tan^{-1}$ means inverse tangent, not a reciprocal.

options.text: Inverse trig works backwards from a side ratio to find a side length; $\tan^{-1}$ does not mean inverse tangent.
options.explanation: Both completions confuse inverse functions with finding sides. Inverse trig finds an angle from a ratio, and $\tan^{-1}$ means inverse tangent rather than one divided by tangent.

cards.front: For angle $ABC$, which point is the angle at?

options.explanation: In angle $ABC$, the middle letter identifies the vertex where the angle is formed, so the angle is at point $B$.
The first letter names one arm of the angle, not its vertex. In angle $ABC$, the middle letter is the vertex, so the angle is at point $B$.
The final letter names the other arm of the angle, not its vertex. In angle $ABC$, the middle letter identifies the vertex, so the angle is at point $B$.
An angle is located at a single vertex, not along a side such as $AC$. In angle $ABC$, the middle letter shows that the vertex is point $B$.

cards.front: Triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $B$, $BC=20\text{ cm}$ and angle $C=35^\circ$. What equation finds $AB$?

options.explanation: Relative to angle $C$, $AB$ is the opposite side and $BC=20$ is the adjacent side. Therefore, tangent gives opposite over adjacent: $\tan 35^\circ=\frac{AB}{20}$.
Sine compares opposite with the hypotenuse, but $20$ is the adjacent side here. The correct ratio uses tangent: $\tan 35^\circ=\frac{AB}{20}$.
This reverses the tangent ratio, using adjacent over opposite instead of opposite over adjacent. The correct equation is $\tan 35^\circ=\frac{AB}{20}$.
Cosine compares adjacent with the hypotenuse, whereas $AB$ is opposite angle $C$ and $20$ is adjacent. The correct equation is $\tan 35^\circ=\frac{AB}{20}$.

cards.front: A trapezium has vertical sides $4\text{ m}$ and $6\text{ m}$. What is the small triangle’s vertical height?

options.explanation: The small triangle’s vertical height is the difference between the two vertical sides: $6-4=2\text{ m}$.
Adding the two vertical sides gives the total of both lengths, not the height difference forming the small triangle. The required height is $6-4=2\text{ m}$.
Averaging the two vertical sides does not find the extra height of the small triangle. Subtract the shorter side from the longer side to get $6-4=2\text{ m}$.
Using the shorter vertical side ignores the additional height represented by the difference between the sides. The small triangle’s vertical height is $6-4=2\text{ m}$.

cards.front: Small right triangle: opposite $2\text{ m}$, adjacent $15\text{ m}$. What equation finds the angle $\theta$ above the horizontal?

options.explanation: For the angle above the horizontal, the vertical side of $2\text{ m}$ is opposite and the horizontal side of $15\text{ m}$ is adjacent. Tangent is opposite over adjacent.
Sine requires the hypotenuse, but $15\text{ m}$ is the adjacent horizontal side. Since the given sides are opposite and adjacent, the correct equation is $\tan\theta=\frac{2}{15}$.
The sides have been placed in the reverse order, giving adjacent over opposite. Tangent uses opposite over adjacent, so the correct equation is $\tan\theta=\frac{2}{15}$.
Cosine compares adjacent with hypotenuse, not opposite with adjacent. Here the relevant ratio is tangent, giving $\tan\theta=\frac{2}{15}$.

cards.front: If the angle to the horizontal is $7.6^\circ$, what is the angle to the vertical?

options.explanation: The horizontal and vertical directions are perpendicular, so their angles add to $90^\circ$. Thus the angle to the vertical is $90-7.6=82.4^\circ$.
Adding $7.6^\circ$ to $90^\circ$ gives the reflex-style value $97.6^\circ$, but the acute complementary angle is required. It is $90-7.6=82.4^\circ$.
The angle to the vertical is not equal to the angle to the horizontal because the reference directions are perpendicular. The two angles are complementary, giving $90-7.6=82.4^\circ$.
Subtracting $7.6^\circ$ from $180^\circ$ finds a supplementary angle, not the angle between the line and the vertical. The required complementary angle is $82.4^\circ$.

cards.front: When asked for 1 decimal place, keep the [ ___ ] and round only at the [ ___ ].
cards.back: When asked for 1 decimal place, keep the full calculator value and round only at the final line.

options.text: When asked for 1 decimal place, keep the full calculator value and round only at the final line.
options.explanation: Keeping the full calculator value avoids cumulative rounding errors. Round only the final result to 1 decimal place, after all calculations have been completed.

options.text: When asked for 1 decimal place, keep the first decimal place and round only at the first step.
options.explanation: Rounding at the first step can change later calculations and produce an inaccurate final answer. Keep the full calculator value and round only at the final line.

options.text: When asked for 1 decimal place, keep the full calculator value and round only at the first step.
options.explanation: Although retaining the full value initially is correct, rounding at the first step introduces avoidable error into subsequent work. Round only at the final line.

options.text: When asked for 1 decimal place, keep the first decimal place and round only at the final line.
options.explanation: Keeping only one decimal place discards useful calculator accuracy before the calculation is finished. Keep the full calculator value, then round only at the final line.

cards.front: A right triangle gives both shorter sides and asks for the hypotenuse. Which method is quickest?

options.explanation: When both shorter sides of a right-angled triangle are known, Pythagoras’ theorem finds the hypotenuse directly using $a^2+b^2=c^2$.
The sine rule is mainly used when the triangle is not necessarily right-angled and includes known opposite side-angle pairs. For two shorter sides of a right triangle, use Pythagoras.
The cosine rule can find a missing side but is unnecessary here and is usually used for non-right-angled triangles. With both shorter sides known in a right triangle, use Pythagoras.
SOHCAHTOA relates a side to a known acute angle, but no angle is needed when both shorter sides are given. Pythagoras is the quickest method for finding the hypotenuse.
